Your Shopping Cart Experience

When shopping for diamonds, understanding the 4 Cs—cut, color, clarity, and carat weight—is crucial. Each characteristic plays a significant role in the overall appearance and value of the diamond. For instance, a well-cut diamond can enhance brilliance and sparkle, making it more visually appealing. Additionally, color grading helps assess how colorless or tinted a diamond is, with the best diamonds being nearly colorless. Clarity refers to the presence of inclusions or blemishes, while carat weight correlates with the size of the diamond. We can delve deeper into each of these characteristics to understand how they affect the choice and pricing of diamonds.

Furthermore, the shopping experience itself is essential for customers looking to purchase diamonds or diamond jewelry. A secure and user-friendly online checkout process fosters confidence in buyers. It is important to ensure that payment gateways are encrypted and that customers' personal information is protected. Providing multiple payment options can also enhance the checkout experience. For instance, offering services like PayPal, credit cards, and financing options can cater to varied customer preferences, ensuring that more buyers can successfully complete their purchases.

In addition to the practical aspects of the shopping cart and checkout process, adding customer reviews and testimonials can bolster trust. Potential buyers often look for social proof before making significant purchases. By displaying reviews from previous customers, prospective buyers can feel more secure in their decision to choose your store over others. It’s worthwhile to consider how testimonials can be integrated into product pages and the checkout process, thereby promoting a more comprehensive sense of trust and reliability.

Lastly, incorporating educational content about diamonds, such as guides on how to choose the perfect diamond, can also boost SEO efforts. By providing valuable information, your website becomes a resource for customers, which can lead to increased traffic and higher conversion rates. This content can include topics such as the different settings available for diamond rings, tips for maintaining the brilliance of diamonds, and popular diamond shapes. By answering common questions and providing detailed insights, you can enhance customer satisfaction and encourage repeat visits to your website.

title: Refund and Returns Policy
content_html:
Effective Date: 7-10-204

At Sothis Diamonds, customer satisfaction is our priority. We take great care in ensuring that every diamond and jewelry piece meets the highest standards of quality and authenticity. This Refund & Return Policy explains how returns, refunds, and exchanges are handled.

1. Eligibility for Returns

You may request a return if:

  • The item is unused, unworn, and in original condition.

  • The return request is made within 14 days of delivery.

  • The item is accompanied by its original packaging, certificates, and invoices.

❌ Returns are not accepted for:

  • Customized or engraved jewelry.

  • Items purchased on sale or promotion (unless defective).

  • Items damaged due to misuse or mishandling after delivery.

2. Return Process

  1. Contact our customer support team at [Insert Email / Phone] within the return window.

  2. Provide order details and reason for return.

  3. Our team will arrange for secure courier pickup or provide instructions for shipping.

  4. Once the item is received and inspected, we will notify you of the approval or rejection of your return.

3. Refunds

  • Approved refunds will be processed to your original payment method within 7–10 business days.

  • Shipping, insurance, and handling fees are non-refundable.

  • For international customers, currency conversion or bank charges may apply.

4. Exchanges

  • Items may be exchanged for another product of equal or higher value (price difference to be paid by customer).

  • Exchanges follow the same inspection and eligibility rules as returns.

5. Damaged or Incorrect Items

If you receive a damaged or incorrect item:

  • Report it to us within 48 hours of delivery.

  • Provide photos/videos of the product and packaging.

  • We will arrange a replacement or full refund at no additional cost.

6. Secure Returns

Since jewelry and diamonds are high-value items, all returns must be:

  • Shipped via insured courier services recommended by us.

  • Packed securely in original packaging.

7. Contact Us

For return or refund requests, please reach us at:

By providing this information, we comply with the European Directive 2009/136/CE and the Telecom Law of July 10, 2012, which require website owners to inform visitors about the use of cookies.

What Are Cookies?

Cookies are small text files that store information about your browsing behavior. While generated by the website server, cookies are saved automatically on your computer, smartphone, or tablet.

There are two main types:

  • Temporary (Session) Cookies – deleted automatically once you close your browser.

  • Persistent (Permanent) Cookies – remain stored until they expire or you delete them.

How Can You Manage Cookies?

You can modify your cookie preferences directly from your internet browser settings.

Resources for popular browsers:

  • Google Chrome

  • Internet Explorer

  • Mozilla Firefox

  • Safari

Types of Cookies We Use

To improve your experience on sothisdiamonds.com, we use:

  1. Session Cookies

    • Help us remember your actions while browsing, so you don’t have to re-enter the same information on each page.

    • Deleted when you close your browser.

  2. Preference Cookies

    • Store your chosen settings (language, location, browser type) so the site remembers your preferences for future visits.

  3. Analytical Cookies

    • Allow us to understand how visitors interact with our site (time spent, pages visited, traffic sources).

    • Used only for website improvement and user experience.

Do Cookies Collect Personal Data?

No. The cookies used by Sothis Diamonds do not collect or store personal data such as your name, address, or email. They only capture technical and usage data to improve your browsing experience.

title: Sell Your Diamond in Belgium
content_html:
Receiving a fair offer for a diamond begins with understanding what you own and how its present selling value is determined.

A loose diamond, engagement ring, inherited piece or other diamond jewellery may have an original receipt, insurance appraisal or grading report. However, none of these documents automatically establishes what a professional buyer will offer today.

Sothis Diamonds provides a private, no-obligation way to submit your diamond for an initial review. Clear photographs and any available documentation can help the team determine whether a physical inspection should be arranged.

Key Takeaways

  • A diamond’s resale value is different from its original retail price and insurance value.
  • Carat, colour, clarity and cut all matter, but they are not the only factors affecting an offer.
  • Natural and laboratory-grown diamonds belong to different resale markets.
  • A GIA, IGI or HRD Antwerp report can support identification but does not guarantee a selling price.
  • Photographs can support an initial review, but a final offer normally requires physical inspection.
  • You are not required to accept a no-obligation offer.
  • Appointments and insured shipping arrangements should be confirmed before transporting valuable jewellery.

Quick Answer: How Can I Sell My Diamond in Belgium?

The safest starting point is to submit clear photographs, a short description and any available grading report to an experienced diamond buyer. The diamond can then be reviewed according to its verified characteristics, condition and current buyer demand.

If the item appears suitable, Sothis Diamonds can arrange a physical inspection at its Antwerp office or discuss an approved insured-shipping procedure. After verification, you may receive a final market-based offer without any obligation to sell.

Additional Notes

A Diamond Often Carries More Than Financial Value

Selling a diamond is not always a purely financial decision. It may be an engagement ring from a relationship that has ended, an inherited piece whose history is unclear or jewellery that has remained unworn for many years.

A professional selling process should therefore begin with information rather than pressure. You should understand what has been examined, which factors affect the offer and what will happen next before deciding whether to proceed.

Sothis Diamonds evaluates diamonds and diamond jewellery privately from its Antwerp location. The purpose of the first review is to establish what you have and determine whether a more detailed inspection is appropriate.

What Types of Diamonds and Jewellery Can You Submit?

You can request an initial valuation for loose diamonds as well as diamonds set in jewellery. There is no need to remove a stone from its setting before sending photographs or arranging an appointment.

Items submitted for consideration may include:

  • Loose natural diamonds
  • Diamond engagement rings
  • Diamond wedding rings
  • Diamond earrings
  • Diamond pendants and necklaces
  • Diamond bracelets and tennis bracelets
  • Vintage and antique diamond jewellery
  • Fancy-coloured diamonds
  • Inherited jewellery containing one or more diamonds

If you are uncertain whether the stone is natural, laboratory-grown or another gemstone, explain what you know in the enquiry. Professional testing may be required before a meaningful offer can be considered.

How Is the Selling Value of a Diamond Determined?

No single piece of information can establish a reliable selling price. Even two diamonds with the same carat weight may have substantially different values because their quality, proportions, documentation, condition and buyer demand are different.

Carat Weight and Measurements

Carat describes weight, not visual size. A well-proportioned one-carat diamond may appear different from another one-carat stone with more weight hidden in its depth. Exact measurements therefore matter alongside the number printed on a grading report.

Colour and Clarity

Small differences in colour grade can influence demand and value. Clarity must also be examined carefully because the size, type and position of inclusions matter—not simply the letters shown on the report.

A dark inclusion beneath the centre of a diamond may affect desirability differently from a less noticeable inclusion close to the edge.

Cut, Shape and Proportions

Cut quality affects how effectively a diamond handles light. Shape also influences demand. Round, oval, emerald, cushion and other cuts do not necessarily trade at the same price even when their carat weight and broad quality grades are similar.

Natural or Laboratory-Grown Origin

Natural and laboratory-grown diamonds are different market categories. Their origin must be correctly identified before a meaningful valuation can be provided. Visual appearance alone is not a reliable way for an owner to determine origin.

Grading Report

A GIA, IGI or HRD Antwerp report can help confirm important characteristics and make the initial review more precise. However, a grading report describes a diamond; it does not state exactly what a buyer must pay.

Jewellery Setting and Precious Metal

When a diamond is mounted in a ring, pendant, bracelet or pair of earrings, the setting must also be considered. Metal type, weight, workmanship, condition and additional gemstones may contribute to the overall offer.

Current Buyer Demand

Diamond prices are not permanently fixed. Current demand, availability, shape, size, certification, visual appearance and the ease with which a diamond can be matched to a future buyer all influence its resale market.

Example: Why Two One-Carat Diamonds May Receive Different Offers

Consider two round diamonds that both weigh 1.00 carat.

The first has a verifiable grading report, a high colour grade, eye-clean clarity and strong cut proportions. The second has a lower colour grade, visible inclusions, less desirable proportions and no recent documentation.

Although both diamonds are described as “one carat,” they should not be expected to receive the same valuation. Carat weight is only one part of the assessment.

This is also why an accurate offer should not be calculated from a photograph alone. Photographs can support an initial review, but they cannot reliably confirm every inclusion, proportion, treatment or grading characteristic.

This is an illustrative example, not a Sothis Diamonds customer case study.

Insurance Value, Retail Price and Resale Value Are Not the Same

One of the most common surprises for sellers is discovering that an old appraisal or original receipt does not equal the amount a diamond can be sold for today.

Type of Value What It Represents Is It a Realistic Selling Price?
Original retail price The amount paid when the diamond or jewellery was purchased Usually not
Current retail price The advertised price of a comparable new item Not necessarily
Insurance value The estimated cost of replacing a comparable item through a retail channel No
Professional purchase offer What a buyer is prepared to pay after considering the item, demand, risk and resale costs Usually the most relevant figure

For example, an insurance document may give a ring a replacement value of €10,000. That does not mean a professional buyer can resell the same pre-owned ring for €10,000 or offer that amount to its owner.

A transparent buyer should explain this difference rather than using the higher insurance figure to create unrealistic expectations.

How the Sothis Diamond-Selling Process Works

1. Send the Available Information

Complete the valuation enquiry with a short description of the item. Include the approximate carat weight if known and upload clear photographs of the front, side and back of the jewellery.

If you have a GIA, IGI or HRD Antwerp report, include a photograph or PDF. You may also submit an old receipt or appraisal as supporting information.

2. Receive an Initial Expert Review

The available information is reviewed to determine the likely item type, whether sufficient details are present and whether a physical inspection should be arranged.

Any estimate based only on photographs and documents remains preliminary. The diamond’s characteristics and condition must be confirmed before a final offer is made.

3. Arrange an Appointment or Secure Shipment

Depending on your location, you may arrange to present the diamond at the Antwerp office or discuss insured shipping with the Sothis team.

content_html:
Quick Answer: How Much Is My Diamond Worth?

A diamond’s value depends on more than its carat weight. Its natural or laboratory-grown origin, shape, colour, clarity, cut quality, proportions, grading report, fluorescence, condition and current buyer demand can all affect the amount it may achieve when sold.

Our calculator uses the information you provide to create a preliminary resale estimate. This is a useful starting point, but it is not a formal appraisal or a guaranteed purchase offer. Photographs, report verification and physical inspection may be required before Sothis Diamonds can confirm a final market-based offer.

Additional Notes

Why Does the Calculator Show a Range Instead of One Exact Price?

A diamond does not have one universally fixed value. A retailer, insurer, auction house and professional diamond buyer may each be answering a different financial question.

Even when a grading report is available, two diamonds with similar headline grades can differ in measurements, proportions, inclusion placement, fluorescence, condition and overall marketability. Buyer demand also changes over time.

A range communicates this uncertainty more honestly than a precise-looking figure generated before the diamond has been examined. The narrower and more reliable estimate comes after the supplied details have been verified.

The result should therefore be presented as a preliminary resale estimate, never as a certified appraisal, guaranteed price or binding offer.

How the Diamond Valuation Calculator Works

The calculator begins with recognised grading characteristics, but it must go beyond simply multiplying carat weight by a fixed price.

One metric carat equals 200 milligrams, but carat measures weight rather than visual size. Diamonds close to significant weights such as 1.00, 1.50 and 2.00 carats may also enter different pricing categories because larger diamonds are rarer.

Natural or Laboratory-Grown Origin

Natural and laboratory-grown diamonds are genuine diamonds, but they belong to different resale markets. An owner may not be able to identify the origin visually, which is why an “I am not sure” option is necessary.

If origin is unknown, the calculator should request professional testing instead of assuming the diamond is natural.

Carat Weight and Measurements

Carat is an important value factor, but two diamonds of the same weight can appear different in size. A deep stone may carry more of its weight below the setting, while a well-proportioned diamond may have a larger face-up appearance.

Measurements also help an expert compare the entered information with the grading report and the physical stone.

Colour, Clarity and Cut

Colour and clarity grades can change the market category into which a diamond falls. The position and nature of an inclusion can also matter in ways that a simple dropdown cannot fully capture.

Cut quality, proportions, polish and symmetry influence appearance and buyer demand. These factors should be considered together rather than treated as unrelated scores.

Shape and Current Demand

Round, oval, emerald, cushion and other shapes do not always trade at the same price. Availability and buyer demand for a particular combination of shape, size and quality can affect the resale range.

Grading Report

A report from GIA, IGI or HRD Antwerp can make an online estimate more dependable because it provides independently assessed characteristics.

The report number should be verified through the issuing laboratory’s official database whenever possible. A report still does not guarantee the stone’s present condition or resale price because the diamond may have been damaged, altered or recut after the report was issued.

Illustrative Example: Two One-Carat Diamonds

Imagine that two sellers each enter a 1.00-carat round natural diamond into the calculator.

The first diamond has a verifiable grading report showing G colour, VS2 clarity and Excellent cut. The report also contains measurements, polish, symmetry and fluorescence information.

The second diamond is also described as one carat, but its exact colour and clarity are unknown. It remains mounted in an older ring and has no report.

The calculator can create a more defined preliminary range for the first stone because the seller has supplied standardised information. The second stone should not be described as worthless or automatically given a very low estimate. It should be directed to an expert review because its identity, weight and grades still need to be confirmed.

This is why a responsible calculator must treat “unknown” as a request for further examination—not as the lowest possible grade.

This is an illustrative example, not a Sothis customer case study.

Purchase Price, Insurance Value and Resale Value Are Different

If a diamond ring originally cost €8,000, it does not automatically have an €8,000 resale value. The purchase price may have included design, manufacturing, branding, retailer expenses, tax and retail margin.

An insurance appraisal usually estimates what it may cost to replace the jewellery through an appropriate retail channel. A resale valuation instead considers what the item could realistically achieve in the present secondary market.

Type of Value What It Means
Purchase price The amount originally paid, including retail costs and margin
Insurance value The estimated cost of replacing a comparable item through a retail channel
Resale value The amount the item may realistically achieve in the present secondary market

An old receipt or appraisal can still provide useful background information. It simply answers a different question from the one a seller is asking today.

Can I Calculate My Diamond’s Value Without a Certificate?

Yes, you should still be able to begin. Many inherited or older diamonds no longer have their original paperwork.

Enter what you know and select “I am not sure” for the remaining fields. Photographs of the complete item, side profile, underside and visible hallmarks can help Sothis decide what type of inspection is required.

However, a photograph cannot reliably confirm exact colour, clarity, carat weight or natural origin. The result may therefore be a request for expert review rather than an immediate monetary range.

Do not pay for new certification before discussing the diamond with a professional buyer. Depending on the stone’s size, quality and likely market, the cost and time involved may or may not improve the selling outcome.

What If the Diamond Is Still in a Ring?

You do not need to remove it yourself. Attempting to loosen the prongs or push the diamond out of its setting could damage both the stone and the ring.

If the grading report shows the centre diamond’s carat weight and characteristics, enter those details. If the paperwork provides only a total carat weight for all stones, select “I am not sure” for the centre-stone weight.

During a professional examination, Sothis can consider the main diamond, smaller stones, precious metal, workmanship, condition and any brand-related value.

Illustrative Scenario: An Inherited Ring with Limited Information

Suppose you inherit a ring marked “18K,” but there is no receipt or grading report. A relative remembers that it was purchased many years ago, but no one knows the diamond’s weight or origin.

You select “diamond ring,” “origin unknown” and “carat weight unknown.” You then upload photographs of the ring from the front, side and underside, including the hallmark.

The calculator does not invent a price. Instead, it creates a valuation profile and asks for an expert review. After physical inspection, the centre stone and surrounding jewellery can be identified and considered separately.

The absence of paperwork creates a need for verification. It does not prove that the ring is valuable, but it also does not prove that it has no value.

This scenario is illustrative and should not be described as an actual customer transaction.

Why Might the Final Offer Differ from the Online Estimate?

An online calculator works with the information entered by the owner. If the carat weight, colour, clarity or origin is estimated incorrectly, the calculated range may change after inspection.

A physical review may also identify details the calculator cannot see, including:

  • A chip near the girdle or underneath a prong
  • A treatment not mentioned in the form
  • A report that does not match the diamond
  • Cloudiness or other condition concerns
  • An incorrect total carat weight
  • Valuable brand, period or workmanship details

The purpose of the estimate is to help you decide whether to continue—not to replace professional verification.

What Happens After I Calculate the Value?

Once your preliminary result appears, you can choose whether to request an expert-reviewed valuation.

Upload clear photographs and any available grading report. The Sothis team can review the information and advise whether the next step should be an Antwerp appointment or an agreed secure shipping process.

If the diamond proceeds to physical inspection, its characteristics, condition and paperwork can be verified before a final market-based offer is prepared. You remain free to accept or decline the offer.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the diamond valuation calculator free?

Yes. The calculator is available without charge or an obligation to sell. If any additional laboratory or certification service could involve a fee, it should be explained and approved separately.

Does the calculator show retail or resale value?

This calculator is designed to indicate possible resale value for someone considering selling a diamond. It does not display a jewellery shop’s retail price or an insurance replacement value.

Is the calculator result a guaranteed offer?

No. The result is a preliminary range based on the information entered. A final offer may require photographs, report verification and physical inspection.

Can I use the calculator if I do not know the 4Cs?

Yes. Select “I am not sure” for unknown details and upload photographs if you want an initial expert review. The calculator should not force owners to guess grades.

Can the value be calculated from a photograph?

Photographs can help identify the item and its condition, but they cannot reliably confirm all grading characteristics. They support an initial review rather than a guaranteed monetary valuation.

Does a GIA report state what my diamond is worth?

No. GIA reports describe a diamond’s quality and identifying characteristics but do not provide an appraisal value or selling price.

Can I calculate the value of a laboratory-grown diamond?

Yes, but it must be assessed within the laboratory-grown resale market. Natural-diamond pricing must never be applied to a laboratory-grown stone.

Does the setting add value?

It may. Precious-metal weight, condition, workmanship, additional stones and recognised brand provenance can affect the value of the complete item.

Does fluorescence always reduce diamond value?

No. Its effect depends on the diamond and the strength and appearance of the fluorescence. It should not be handled through an automatic universal deduction.

What if my diamond has a chip?

You can still request a valuation. Select the possible-damage option and upload clear photographs. The location and severity of the damage need to be examined before its effect on value can be determined.

Can I use the calculator for fancy-coloured diamonds?

You can submit their information, but fancy-coloured diamonds should be routed to a specialist rather than priced with a standard D-to-Z diamond formula. Colour, intensity, overtone, origin and rarity require individual review.

Do I have to sell after receiving the result?

No. The calculator and initial review are intended to provide information. You decide whether you want to proceed after receiving the final offer.

The Centre Diamond

title: Sell a Loose Diamond in Belgium & Europe
content_html:
Receive a private, market-based offer from an Antwerp diamond specialist.

A loose diamond can often be assessed more precisely than a mounted stone because its complete dimensions, carat weight, condition and identifying characteristics are accessible during inspection.

Whether your diamond was removed from a ring, inherited, purchased as an investment or retained after redesigning a piece of jewellery, Sothis Diamonds can begin with a private online review.

Submit photographs and any available GIA, IGI or HRD Antwerp report. If the diamond meets the current buying criteria, you can arrange an appointment in Antwerp or discuss an agreed insured shipping process from your European location.

The initial review and offer are free. You remain free to accept or decline.

Book an Antwerp Appointment

Private review · Verified assessment · No obligation to sell

Quick Answer: How Can I Sell a Loose Diamond in Belgium or Europe?

To sell a loose diamond, begin by submitting clear photographs of the stone and a complete image or PDF of its grading report, if available. Include the diamond’s shape, carat weight and grading laboratory when known.

The report number can be checked in the issuing laboratory’s database before the physical diamond is examined. During inspection, the stone can be weighed, measured and tested to confirm whether it is natural or laboratory-grown and whether its characteristics correspond with the submitted documentation.

Its colour, clarity, cut, proportions, fluorescence, treatments, condition and current market demand are then considered. After verification, Sothis Diamonds can provide a market-based offer that you are free to accept or decline.

Additional Notes

What Is Considered a Loose Diamond?

A loose diamond is a polished diamond that is not currently mounted in a ring, pendant, bracelet, earring or other piece of jewellery.

It may have been purchased separately, removed professionally from an older setting, inherited in a diamond paper or retained following a jewellery redesign. A loose diamond may be certified or uncertified, natural or laboratory-grown, colourless or fancy coloured.

This page concerns polished gem-quality diamonds. Rough, uncut and industrial diamonds involve different identification, documentation and trading considerations and should be submitted as a separate enquiry before any appointment or shipment is arranged.

If your diamond remains mounted in jewellery, use the relevant sell a diamond ring or sell an engagement ring page. Do not remove it yourself merely to use this service.

What Types of Loose Diamonds Can Be Submitted?

Sothis Diamonds can begin an initial review of different loose-diamond categories, subject to current buying criteria.

These may include:

  • GIA, IGI or HRD Antwerp graded diamonds
  • Uncertified polished diamonds
  • Natural loose diamonds
  • Laboratory-grown loose diamonds
  • Round, oval, emerald, cushion, pear, radiant, princess and marquise shapes
  • Natural fancy-coloured diamonds
  • Diamonds removed from rings or other jewellery
  • Inherited or estate diamonds
  • Older European-cut and antique-cut diamonds
  • Individual diamonds and small groups of stones
  • Diamonds with chips, abrasion or other condition concerns

Not every submitted diamond will necessarily receive an offer. Very small stones, heavily damaged diamonds, simulants, certain treated stones and commercial parcels may fall outside the current buying criteria.

State what you know and leave unknown fields unanswered rather than estimating grades from appearance.

How Selling a Loose Diamond Works

1. Submit the Diamond’s Details

Begin with the shape, approximate carat weight, grading laboratory and report number when available. If you are uncertain whether the stone is natural or laboratory-grown, select “unknown.”

Include how the diamond came into your possession, but only to the extent required to establish ownership and identify any relevant documentation.

2. Upload Photographs and the Grading Report

Photograph the diamond securely inside a transparent gem container or unopened diamond paper. Do not balance it on an exposed table, hold it with improvised tools or place it close to a sink or floor edge.

Upload the complete grading report rather than only the page showing the 4Cs. The measurements, proportions, comments, plotting diagram and inscription information may all be relevant.

3. Receive an Initial Review

The report number can be checked against the issuing laboratory’s online records. GIA’s Report Check allows the recorded report information to be compared with its archived data, while HRD Antwerp provides access to its report archive through My HRD Antwerp. GIA Report Check and My HRD Antwerp.

This confirms that report data exists in the laboratory archive. It does not, by itself, prove that the physical diamond submitted is the same stone.

4. Arrange Physical Inspection

Sellers in Belgium can arrange a private Antwerp appointment. Sellers elsewhere in Europe can ask whether insured collection or shipping is available from their location.

Do not send the diamond until the carrier, declared value, insurance coverage, packaging, tracking, inspection period and return arrangements have been confirmed in writing.

5. Receive Your Market-Based Offer

After inspection, Sothis Diamonds can prepare an offer based on the verified diamond and current market conditions.

The offer should state whether it is final, how long it remains valid, whether any deductions apply and how payment will be completed. You can accept or decline without pressure.

Start My Loose-Diamond Review

How Is a Loose Diamond Offer Calculated?

A diamond’s value cannot be determined responsibly from its carat weight or grading report alone. The complete combination of characteristics must be considered.

Carat Weight

Carat measures weight rather than visible size. One metric carat equals 0.20 grams. Prices per carat do not increase in a perfectly straight line, and diamonds above commercially important weight thresholds can trade differently from stones just below them. GIA Diamond Buyer’s Guide.

Because the stone is loose, it can be weighed directly rather than estimating its weight from measurements.

Colour and Clarity

Colour and clarity grades influence rarity and demand, but neither should be considered in isolation.

The location and visibility of clarity characteristics may affect how attractive a diamond appears and how easily it can be resold. Two diamonds with the same clarity grade can therefore receive different offers.

Cut, Proportions and Visual Performance

For standard round brilliant diamonds, a laboratory cut grade provides useful information. Table percentage, depth, crown and pavilion relationships, polish and symmetry may also influence appearance and demand.

Fancy-shaped diamonds require more individual assessment because their outline, length-to-width ratio, bow-tie effect, symmetry and face-up appearance can vary substantially even when the report grades appear similar.

Shape and Current Demand

Round, oval, emerald, cushion, pear, radiant and other shapes do not necessarily achieve the same price per carat.

Demand also changes according to the combination of shape, weight, colour, clarity and proportions. A technically attractive diamond may still have a narrower resale market if its shape or proportions are currently less sought after.

Fluorescence

Fluorescence is considered together with the rest of the diamond. Its effect can depend on its strength, colour and how the stone appears under different lighting.

The presence of fluorescence should not automatically be described as either positive or negative without examining the individual diamond.

Natural or Laboratory-Grown Origin

Natural and laboratory-grown diamonds can appear similar, but they operate within separate resale markets.

A grading report may document the diamond’s growth origin. When the origin is unknown or the report cannot be verified, specialist testing may be required before a final offer can be prepared.

Growth origin should not be confused with geographic mine origin. A normal grading report does not necessarily establish the country in which a natural diamond was mined.

Treatments and Condition

Laser drilling, fracture filling, high-pressure high-temperature processing and other treatments can affect marketability and must be disclosed when known.

The diamond is also examined for chips, cavities, abrasion, damaged points, girdle wear and signs of repolishing. A damaged diamond may still have value, but repair or recutting risks must be considered.

Grading Report and Identification

A current, verifiable GIA, IGI or HRD Antwerp report can make the diamond easier to identify and compare.

GIA explains that its grading reports include an assessment of a loose diamond’s quality characteristics, measurements and known treatments. The report is not a monetary appraisal and does not dictate what a buyer will pay. GIA grading-report information.

Present Market Demand

The final offer reflects the market available at the time of assessment. Original retail price, insurance value and a previous appraisal may provide background, but they do not establish today’s purchase price.

Illustrative Example: A Certified Loose Natural Diamond

Imagine that a seller submits a loose 1.30-carat oval natural diamond with a GIA report recording F colour and VS2 clarity.

The seller also provides the original retail invoice. The report number is found in GIA’s database, but the physical stone must still be examined.

During inspection, the diamond is weighed and measured. Its outline, proportions, clarity characteristics, fluorescence, inscription and condition are compared with the report. The specialist also assesses whether its length-to-width ratio, bow-tie effect and face-up appearance suit current market demand.

The resulting offer reflects the verified diamond and its present resale market. It may be substantially lower than the original retail invoice because the retail and secondary-market figures serve different purposes.

This is an illustrative example and should not be presented as an actual Sothis Diamonds transaction.

Can I Sell a Certified Loose Diamond?

Yes. A recognised grading report can make the initial assessment more accurate because it records characteristics that would otherwise need to be established through physical examination.

GIA issues its Diamond Grading Report for loose natural diamonds, while HRD Antwerp describes its Natural Diamond Grading Report as an objective report confirming authenticity and the 4Cs. GIA diamond-grading services and HRD Antwerp Natural Diamond Grading Report.

The report number should first be verified online. The physical stone must then be compared with the recorded weight, measurements, shape, plotting diagram and inscription.

A genuine report offered beside an unrelated diamond does not make the diamond certified. The report and stone must belong together.

What If the Diamond Has a Laser Inscription?

A microscopic inscription on the girdle may show a laboratory report number or other identifying information.

GIA explains that a report-number inscription can help match a diamond with its documentation. It is normally viewed under magnification and checked alongside the report’s other identifying information. GIA laser-inscription guidance.

The presence of a number is useful, but it should not be treated as the only identification step. The inscription, measurements, weight and internal characteristics should be considered together.

Do not attempt to clean, polish, alter or deepen an inscription before assessment.

Can I Sell a Loose Diamond Without a Certificate?

Yes. An uncertified loose diamond can still be submitted for review.

Physical testing may be needed to confirm that the stone is a diamond, establish whether it is natural or laboratory-grown and assess its approximate quality and condition.

For certain stones, obtaining a recognised laboratory report may improve marketability. However, certification involves fees, transport and processing time, and it may not be commercially worthwhile for every diamond.

Loose stones already meet the physical format required for laboratory grading, but do not submit the diamond independently before receiving advice. Sothis Diamonds can first assess whether a new report is likely to improve the selling outcome.

Can I Sell a Laboratory-Grown Loose Diamond?

You can submit a laboratory-grown diamond for review, but it must be assessed within the laboratory-grown resale market and Sothis Diamonds’ current buying criteria.

Laboratory-grown diamonds should not be valued using natural-diamond price assumptions. Their report, production method, age, size, quality, condition and present demand may influence whether an offer is possible.

If the origin is uncertain, do not describe the diamond as natural merely because it was expensive or purchased several years ago. Submit the documentation and allow the stone to be tested.

Can I Sell a Fancy-Coloured Loose Diamond?

Natural pink, blue, yellow, green and other fancy-coloured diamonds require specialised assessment.

The strength, distribution and origin of the colour can have a substantial effect on value. A natural colour, treated colour and laboratory-grown colour should not be treated as equivalent.

A recognised coloured-diamond report may record whether the colour is natural and describe its grade. If no appropriate report is available, further laboratory testing may be recommended before a final offer is made.

Avoid describing a pale yellow D-to-Z diamond as a “fancy yellow” diamond unless the grading supports that classification.

Can I Sell Several Loose Diamonds Together?

Yes. Submit the number of diamonds, their individual weights and the available reports.

A matched pair of diamonds may be assessed differently from two unrelated stones, particularly when the shapes, dimensions, colour and clarity are closely aligned. A group of small diamonds may be valued as a parcel rather than by preparing a separate retail-style price for every stone.

Keep each diamond in an individually labelled compartment or secure diamond paper. Reports and report numbers should be matched clearly to the relevant stones.

Do not mix certified and uncertified diamonds loosely in the same container.

Selling a Loose Diamond from Another European Country

Sothis Diamonds is based in Antwerp, but sellers may begin an enquiry from elsewhere in Europe.

Sellers in the Netherlands, France, Germany, Luxembourg and other EU countries can submit photographs and documents before deciding whether to travel or request shipping information.

The EU customs union generally allows goods to move between EU member states without customs duties at internal borders. However, this does not remove the need for secure transport, accurate ownership information, insurance or any transaction documentation required by the buyer. European Union customs guidance.

Countries such as the United Kingdom, Switzerland and Norway are in Europe but are not EU member states. Cross-border shipments to Belgium may therefore involve customs declarations, import procedures, taxes or temporary-import arrangements.

Do not assume that a standard courier label is sufficient. Before sending from a non-EU country, confirm the process with Sothis Diamonds, the carrier and the relevant customs authority. The diamond’s description and value must never be deliberately understated.

How to Ship a Loose Diamond Safely

Do not send a loose diamond through ordinary, uninsured post.

Before dispatch, confirm:

  • Whether Sothis Diamonds has agreed to receive the item
  • Which carrier and service can accept loose precious stones
  • The maximum insurance coverage
  • How the declared value will be established
  • Whether collection is available
  • Required customs documents
  • Who is responsible during transit
  • How the diamond will be returned if you decline
  • Whether the package must remain unopened until recorded inspection

Place the diamond in a secure gem container or properly folded diamond paper. Put that container inside a tamper-evident inner package and a strong, discreet outer package.

Do not write “diamond,” “jewellery” or other descriptions of valuable contents on the visible exterior unless the approved carrier specifically requires it as part of the declaration process.

Photograph the diamond, report, packaging stages and sealed parcel. Retain the tracking number and handover receipt.

Specific instructions from the approved carrier and Sothis Diamonds should take precedence over general website guidance.

How to Compare Loose-Diamond Offers

Do not compare only the largest preliminary number. Establish what has actually been verified and which deductions may follow.

Ask whether the offer is final after physical inspection or remains conditional upon laboratory testing. Confirm whether grading, shipping, insurance, customs, recutting or other expenses will be deducted.

You should also establish:

  • Whether the report and diamond were physically matched
  • Whether the diamond’s natural or laboratory-grown origin was tested
  • Whether damage or treatments affected the offer
  • How long the offer remains valid
  • When and how payment will be completed
  • What identification is required
  • What happens if you decline
  • Who covers insured return delivery

A clearly explained offer that remains valid after inspection may be more dependable than a high online estimate based only on self-reported grades.

Why Sell a Loose Diamond in Antwerp?

Antwerp continues to provide an established professional market for polished diamonds.

The Antwerp World Diamond Centre reported that Antwerp’s combined diamond imports and exports reached USD 19.07 billion in 2025, with polished diamonds representing 65.6% of that trade value. AWDC 2025 diamond-industry figures.

This does not guarantee a high price for every diamond. It does, however, provide access to an active diamond-trading environment where a loose stone can be inspected in relation to recognised characteristics and present market demand.

Sothis Diamonds is located at:

Hoveniersstraat 2, Bus 210 2018 Antwerp, Belgium

Arrange an appointment before travelling with a valuable diamond.

How to Prepare Your Diamond for Review

Keep the diamond inside its existing gem container or folded diamond paper. Avoid handling it over hard floors, sinks, drains or uncovered surfaces.

For the initial online review, photograph the diamond in indirect daylight while it remains secure. Include the front and back of the grading report and make sure the report number is readable.

Provide:

  • Diamond shape
  • Carat weight, if known
  • Natural, laboratory-grown or unknown origin
  • Laboratory and report number
  • Purchase invoice or previous appraisal, if available
  • Information about damage, treatments or recutting
  • The number of diamonds being submitted
  • Your country and preferred review method

Do not use metal tweezers unless you are experienced in handling loose stones. Do not attempt to photograph the laser inscription if doing so could cause the diamond to be dropped.

A Private and Secure Selling Process

A loose diamond is small, valuable and easily misplaced. Its handling and movement should therefore be documented carefully.

Only authorised reviewers should have access to uploaded reports, photographs and personal information. The seller should receive clear confirmation when the diamond arrives for inspection.

Before transferring ownership, confirm the final offer, payment method, transaction documents and expected payment timeframe. If the offer is declined, the agreed insured return or collection process should be followed.

Receiving an assessment does not oblige you to sell.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the loose-diamond review free?

Yes. The initial review and market-based offer should be free and carry no obligation to sell. Any optional laboratory, shipping or third-party cost should be explained and approved separately.

Do I need a GIA, IGI or HRD report?

No. A verifiable report can make the assessment more precise, but an uncertified loose diamond can still be submitted for review.

Is an online offer final?

An online figure is normally preliminary. A final offer can be confirmed after the physical diamond’s identity, origin, weight, quality, condition and documentation have been verified.

Can I sell a diamond removed from a ring?

Yes, provided it was removed professionally and you are authorised to sell it. Submit any report or information previously associated with the ring.

Should I remove my diamond from its setting before selling?

No. If the diamond remains mounted, submit the complete piece first. Removing it prematurely could damage the stone or reduce the value of a branded, antique or well-crafted ring.

Can I sell a chipped loose diamond?

Potentially. A chip does not automatically remove all value, but its position, severity and possible effect on recutting must be examined.

Can I sell a laboratory-grown loose diamond?

You can submit it for review, but laboratory-grown diamonds are assessed within their own resale market and Sothis Diamonds’ current buying criteria.

Can I sell several loose diamonds?

Yes. Keep the stones separated and match each grading report to the correct diamond whenever possible.

Does a laser inscription guarantee the diamond’s value?

No. An inscription can help identify the stone, but value still depends on the verified characteristics, condition and present market demand.

Is the grading-report value what I will receive?

A grading report does not normally state a monetary value. A purchase offer reflects what the buyer is prepared to pay in the current resale market.

Is an insurance appraisal the same as a selling price?

No. An insurance appraisal generally concerns replacement cost. It does not guarantee the amount the diamond can achieve through resale.

Can I sell a loose diamond from outside Belgium?

Potentially. Begin with an online submission. Sothis Diamonds can then advise whether an Antwerp appointment or an agreed insured shipping process is available for your country.

Can I ship a diamond from the United Kingdom or Switzerland?

Potentially, but these are outside the EU customs union. Customs, insurance and carrier requirements must be confirmed before dispatch.

Should I clean the diamond first?

A gentle professional cleaning may improve visibility, but it is not required for the initial submission. Do not use risky chemicals or handle the stone insecurely merely to clean it.

How quickly will I receive an offer?

The timeframe depends on the information provided and whether physical inspection or additional testing is required. The expected timing should be confirmed following the initial review.

How will payment be made?

The payment method, transaction documents and payment timeframe should be confirmed before ownership is transferred.

Can I visit Sothis Diamonds in Antwerp?

Yes. Arrange a private appointment before travelling so the appropriate specialist is available.

title: Sell a Diamond Without a Certificate
content_html:
You may still be able to sell your diamond when its GIA, IGI or HRD Antwerp report has been lost, damaged or was never issued.

A missing certificate does not make a genuine diamond worthless. It does mean that the stone’s identity, natural or laboratory-grown origin, carat weight, quality characteristics, treatments and condition may need to be established before a final offer can be confirmed.

Sothis Diamonds can begin with a private online review. Submit photographs of the diamond or complete piece of jewellery, along with any receipt, appraisal, old photograph, report number or other information you still have.

If the item meets the current buying criteria, the next step may be a private appointment in Antwerp or an agreed insured shipping process. You remain free to accept or decline the final offer.

Book an Antwerp Appointment

No certificate required · Private review · No obligation to sell

Quick Answer: Can You Sell a Diamond Without a Certificate?

Yes. A diamond can potentially be sold without its original grading certificate.

The buyer must first confirm that the stone is a diamond rather than a simulant and determine whether it is natural, laboratory-grown or treated. Its approximate carat weight, colour, clarity, cut, measurements and condition must then be assessed.

A mounted diamond can usually receive an initial review without being removed. However, a precise laboratory grading report normally requires a loose stone because the setting can obscure the diamond and prevent exact weighing.

For a larger or commercially desirable diamond, a new report from a recognised laboratory may improve identification and marketability. It is not automatically worthwhile for every stone. The likely benefit should be considered against the cost, time, transport and any professional removal or resetting required.

Additional Notes

“Certificate” and “Grading Report” Do Not Mean Exactly the Same Thing

People commonly use the term “diamond certificate,” but recognised laboratories generally issue grading or identification reports.

A grading report records technical information about the examined stone. Depending on the laboratory and service, this can include its natural or laboratory-grown origin, shape, measurements, carat weight, colour, clarity, cut, polish, symmetry, fluorescence, treatments and identifying characteristics.

GIA specifically explains that it does not certify or appraise diamonds. Its reports provide technical information but do not state a monetary value. GIA explanation of grading reports

A report is therefore different from:

  • A shop receipt showing the original purchase price
  • An insurance appraisal estimating replacement cost
  • A jewellery valuation prepared for probate or another purpose
  • A manufacturer’s warranty
  • A brand authenticity card
  • A document produced by the seller rather than an independent laboratory

These documents may provide useful background, but none should automatically be treated as an independent diamond grading report.

What Types of Uncertified Diamonds Can Be Submitted?

You can begin an enquiry for a diamond that has never been graded, as well as one whose original paperwork has been lost.

Potential submissions include:

  • Loose natural diamonds without reports
  • Diamond rings without certificates
  • Engagement rings with missing paperwork
  • Inherited or estate diamonds
  • Older diamonds purchased before modern grading reports became common
  • Antique and old-cut diamonds
  • Diamonds removed professionally from jewellery
  • Laboratory-grown diamonds with missing reports
  • Fancy-coloured diamonds without current documentation
  • Chipped or worn diamonds
  • Branded jewellery without its original papers
  • Groups of small diamonds or matched stones

Not every item will necessarily qualify for an offer. Very small diamonds, simulants, heavily damaged stones, some treated diamonds and certain laboratory-grown diamonds may fall outside current buying criteria.

Do not guess the colour, clarity or origin. It is better to select “unknown” and allow the stone to be examined.

How Selling a Diamond Without a Certificate Works

1. Submit What You Know

Begin with clear photographs of the complete item. State whether the diamond is loose or mounted and include any information you remember about its approximate size, purchase date, jeweller or grading laboratory.

If the diamond was inherited, you do not need to know where it was originally purchased.

2. Provide Any Remaining Evidence

A complete certificate is not the only useful evidence. An old report number, invoice, appraisal, insurance schedule, branded box, repair record or photograph of the original paperwork may help identify the item.

Upload the document in full. Do not hide dates, comments or grades that appear less favourable.

3. Search for Existing Digital Report Data

If you still have a report number, the laboratory’s online database may contain the grading information.

GIA Report Check allows users to compare a report number with information in the GIA archive. GIA states that it does not issue duplicate reports, but reports dated after 1 July 2010 may have a downloadable PDF available through Report Check. Replacing a lost GIA report

IGI provides an online report-verification service, while My HRD Antwerp gives access to HRD Antwerp’s grading-report archive. HRD Antwerp states that digital copies of reports issued after 2013 are generally retained in its database for ten years. IGI report verification and HRD Antwerp report services

Finding digital data is useful, but it does not prove that the physical diamond is the stone described. Its weight, measurements, internal characteristics and any laser inscription must still be compared where possible.

4. Arrange Physical Examination

The diamond must be tested and inspected before a final offer can be confirmed.

Sellers in Belgium can arrange a private appointment in Antwerp. Sellers elsewhere in Europe can first submit photographs and ask whether insured collection or shipping is available from their location.

Do not send valuable jewellery or a loose diamond until the carrier, insurance, packaging, declared value, inspection period and return terms have been agreed in writing.

5. Decide Whether Additional Grading Is Needed

Some diamonds can be assessed and offered for directly. Others may benefit from a recognised laboratory report before a final offer or broader resale strategy is established.

If additional grading is suggested, the reason, laboratory, expected cost, transport process and estimated timeframe should be explained first. No optional third-party service should be ordered without the seller’s agreement.

6. Receive the Offer

After the diamond has been verified, Sothis Diamonds can prepare a market-based offer.

The offer should clarify whether laboratory, removal, shipping or other authorised expenses will be deducted. You should also be told how long the offer remains valid, how payment will be made and what happens if you decline.

Start My Uncertified-Diamond Review

How Is a Diamond Assessed Without Its Certificate?

A missing report means that the buyer cannot safely rely on the grades remembered or supplied by the owner. The stone must be assessed on its current, verifiable characteristics.

Diamond, Simulant or Another Gemstone

The first step is confirming what the stone actually is.

Diamond simulants such as cubic zirconia and moissanite can resemble diamonds to an untrained observer. A simple handheld tester may form part of an initial examination, but more advanced equipment can be required to establish the material and its growth origin reliably.

Natural or Laboratory-Grown Origin

Natural and laboratory-grown diamonds have essentially the same crystal structure and can look similar. Visual inspection alone is not a responsible basis for declaring an uncertified stone natural.

Specialist screening or laboratory testing may be required. Natural and laboratory-grown diamonds must then be valued within their separate resale markets.

Carat Weight and Measurements

A loose diamond can be weighed directly. A mounted diamond’s weight may need to be estimated from accessible measurements until professional removal is considered.

One carat equals 0.20 grams, but carat measures weight rather than visible diameter. Shape, proportions and depth influence how large a diamond appears.

Colour and Clarity

Colour and clarity can be estimated during an initial assessment, but a mounting may influence what can be observed.

Metal colour, surrounding stones, dirt, prongs and the enclosed parts of the diamond can all affect the examination. Any preliminary grade for a mounted stone should therefore be described as an estimate or range rather than presented as a laboratory-confirmed grade.

Cut and Proportions

Cut quality influences the appearance and demand for a diamond.

For a round brilliant, table, depth, crown and pavilion relationships, polish, symmetry and light performance may be considered. Fancy shapes such as oval, pear, emerald, cushion and radiant diamonds require assessment of their outline, proportions, symmetry and visible effects such as bow-ties or windowing.

Treatments

Some diamonds have received treatments intended to alter their apparent colour or clarity.

Known treatments should be disclosed. Where the stone’s history is uncertain, specialist examination may be necessary because treatments can affect marketability and the type of report available.

Condition

Chips, cavities, abrasion, worn facet edges, damaged points and signs of repolishing can influence the offer.

A damaged diamond may still retain value, but the cost and risk of possible recutting must be considered. Do not have the diamond polished or recut merely to obtain an offer unless the commercial reason has been explained.

Current Market Demand

Once the diamond has been identified and assessed, its combination of size, origin, shape, colour, clarity, proportions and condition is considered against current demand.

The original retail price and an old insurance value do not determine what the diamond can be sold for today.

Does Having No Certificate Reduce the Diamond’s Value?

The missing paper does not physically change the diamond. However, the lack of independent information can affect how confidently and efficiently it can be traded.

A buyer may need to account for testing, grading uncertainty, professional removal, laboratory fees, insured transport and the time required to establish the stone’s characteristics. Until these questions are resolved, an online figure may be more conservative or remain conditional.

For a larger, high-quality or unusual diamond, recognised documentation may improve marketability enough to justify additional grading. For a small, damaged or lower-demand stone, the cost of a new report may not be recovered through the selling price.

The correct question is therefore not simply, “Will a certificate increase the value?” It is, “Will obtaining reliable grading information improve the net selling result after all costs and risks?”

Should I Get a New Certificate Before Selling?

Do not automatically send the diamond to a laboratory before obtaining an initial specialist review.

A new report may be worthwhile when:

  • The diamond is sufficiently valuable for precise grading to affect the market
  • Its natural or laboratory-grown origin requires independent confirmation
  • It is a fancy-coloured diamond whose colour origin is important
  • The previous report cannot be recovered
  • The diamond has been repolished or altered since its earlier grading
  • The available information is too uncertain for a final offer

It may not be worthwhile when the diamond is very small, heavily damaged, already clearly outside the buyer’s criteria or worth less than the combined grading and handling costs.

GIA’s standard full grading reports for D-to-Z natural diamonds are intended for loose stones. GIA explains that a setting can obscure colour and clarity and prevent an exact carat-weight determination. Why GIA grades diamonds loose

Before agreeing to new grading, confirm:

  • Which laboratory will examine the diamond
  • Whether the stone must be removed from its setting
  • Who will perform and insure the removal
  • Who will pay the grading and transport costs
  • Whether those costs apply if you decline the offer
  • How long the process is expected to take
  • What happens if the result is different from the expected grade

Can a Lost Certificate Be Recovered?

Sometimes the grading information can be recovered even when the paper document is missing.

Start by checking old emails, purchase invoices, insurance schedules, repair records and photographs. The report number may also appear as a microscopic inscription on the diamond’s girdle.

If a number is found, it can be searched through the relevant laboratory’s official verification service. Never rely on an image of a report found on an unofficial website.

GIA does not issue duplicate reports. However, it may provide archived data—and for qualifying reports, a PDF—through Report Check. HRD Antwerp currently lists duplicate-report and update services under specific conditions, while IGI allows report details to be searched online.

Policies, eligibility, fees and record-retention periods can change. The issuing laboratory should confirm what is available for the specific report.

Most importantly, recovered report data must still be matched to the physical diamond. A valid report number offered beside a different stone does not authenticate that stone.

What If the Report Number Is Inscribed on the Diamond?

Some graded diamonds carry a microscopic report number on the girdle.

A specialist may be able to locate the inscription under magnification and search it in the issuing laboratory’s database. Measurements, weight and internal characteristics should then be compared with the archived report.

An inscription is useful identification evidence, but it should not be treated as the only verification step. Inscriptions can be difficult to read, altered, removed during repolishing or copied fraudulently.

Do not attempt to polish the girdle, deepen the inscription or remove the diamond yourself.

Can I Sell a Mounted Diamond Without a Certificate?

Yes. Submit the complete ring or jewellery item in its current condition.

An initial review can consider the diamond’s approximate size, shape, visible quality, condition, setting, precious-metal content, smaller stones, brand and overall craftsmanship.

IGI notes that mounted-jewellery grading may need to express colour and clarity as ranges because the setting limits what can be examined. IGI jewellery-report information

If exact weighing or full laboratory grading is commercially justified, professional removal may be discussed. However, removing the centre stone too early could damage the diamond or reduce the value of a branded, antique or well-crafted piece as complete jewellery.

Do Not Remove the Diamond Yourself

Do not bend prongs, cut the setting or attempt to push the diamond out using household tools.

An improvised removal can chip the stone, damage its girdle, distort the setting or cause a small diamond to be lost. It may also eliminate the possibility of selling a desirable ring as a complete piece.

If removal is necessary, the diamond and setting should first be examined by an appropriately qualified professional. The risks, cost, insurance responsibility and resetting arrangements should be agreed before work begins.

Can I Sell an Inherited Diamond Without Paperwork?

Yes. Inherited diamonds frequently arrive with incomplete or outdated documentation.

Preserve everything found with the item, including its box, receipt, valuation, repair record, handwritten note, photograph and insurance schedule. This information may help establish provenance or identify a recognised jewellery house.

Age and family history do not automatically create high market value. Equally, the absence of paperwork does not mean the stone has little value. Its material, origin, quality, condition and current demand must still be established.

If several people have an interest in the inherited property, confirm who has legal authority to approve the sale before submitting or transferring the item.

Is an Appraisal Enough to Sell the Diamond?

An appraisal is useful background, but it is not the same as a grading report or purchase offer.

Many insurance appraisals estimate the cost of replacing the diamond or jewellery through a retail environment. That figure may include retail margins, taxes, craftsmanship and the cost of recreating the complete piece.

A resale offer reflects what a buyer is prepared to pay for the verified item in the present secondary market. It may therefore be substantially lower than an insurance value.

GIA confirms that its grading reports do not include monetary appraisal values, although the independently assessed quality characteristics can be used by others when determining value. GIA appraisal guidance

Can I Sell a Laboratory-Grown Diamond Without a Certificate?

You can submit a laboratory-grown diamond without its report, but it must be assessed within the laboratory-grown resale market and Sothis Diamonds’ current buying criteria.

Do not assume a diamond is natural because it was expensive, inherited or purchased many years ago. Laboratory-grown origin cannot always be determined through ordinary visual examination.

Testing may be required before an offer is possible. If the diamond proves to be laboratory-grown, it should not be valued using natural-diamond price assumptions.

Can I Sell a Fancy-Coloured Diamond Without a Certificate?

Potentially, but additional care is required.

The value of a pink, blue, yellow, green or other coloured diamond can depend heavily on whether the colour is natural, treated or produced in a laboratory. Colour strength, distribution and grading terminology also matter.

A recognised coloured-diamond report may therefore be more important than it would be for some ordinary colourless stones. Do not advertise a pale yellow diamond as “fancy yellow” unless appropriate grading supports that description.

Sothis Diamonds can first review the stone and advise whether specialist laboratory examination should be considered.

Can I Sell a Chipped Diamond Without a Certificate?

Potentially. A chip does not automatically eliminate the diamond’s value.

The position and severity of the damage must be examined. A small chip near the girdle may have different commercial implications from a large break affecting the diamond’s face-up appearance or structural security.

Do not recut or repolish the stone before receiving specialist advice. The weight lost during recutting and the risk of moving below an important carat threshold may outweigh the improvement in condition.

Illustrative Example: An Inherited Diamond Ring with No Paperwork

Imagine that a seller inherits a solitaire ring without a receipt or grading report.

The family believes the ring contains a natural diamond of approximately one carat, but no independent evidence is available. The seller submits clear photographs of the ring, hallmarks and complete setting.

During an initial review, the stone’s shape and approximate measurements are recorded. The precious metal and condition of the setting are also considered. A physical appointment is then arranged so the centre stone can be screened and examined.

Testing indicates that it is a natural diamond. Because the mounting prevents exact weighing and grading, the specialist discusses whether professional removal and laboratory grading are commercially worthwhile.

The seller receives an explanation of the expected costs and potential benefit before deciding. The eventual offer is based on the verified stone, setting and current market—not the family’s estimated grade or an assumed retail value.

This is an illustrative example and should not be presented as an actual Sothis Diamonds transaction.

How to Compare Offers for an Uncertified Diamond

Be cautious when comparing offers based on grades that have not been verified.

A high preliminary estimate may change substantially after physical inspection. Ask each buyer what assumptions were used and whether any testing, grading, shipping, insurance or removal expenses will be deducted.

Confirm:

  • Whether the diamond has been physically tested
  • Whether natural or laboratory-grown origin has been established
  • Whether the grades are estimates or laboratory results
  • Whether the setting and smaller stones are included
  • Whether laboratory grading is required
  • Who pays any approved third-party costs
  • Whether the stated amount is final
  • How long the offer remains valid
  • What happens if you decline
  • Who covers insured return delivery
  • When and how payment will be completed

A transparent offer based on verified information may be more dependable than a larger online estimate based only on the seller’s description.

Why Have an Uncertified Diamond Assessed in Antwerp?

Antwerp has an established infrastructure for inspecting, grading and trading polished diamonds.

According to the Antwerp World Diamond Centre, combined imports and exports across Antwerp’s diamond industry reached USD 19.07 billion in 2025, with polished diamonds representing 65.6% of the total trade value. AWDC Antwerp diamond-industry figures

This does not guarantee that every uncertified diamond will receive an offer or achieve a particular price. It does provide access to a professional diamond environment in which an undocumented stone can be assessed against verifiable characteristics and current market demand.

Sothis Diamonds is located at:

Hoveniersstraat 2, Bus 210 2018 Antwerp, Belgium

Arrange a private appointment before travelling with valuable jewellery.

How to Prepare an Uncertified Diamond for Review

Do not have the diamond removed, polished, repaired or laboratory graded before the initial review unless a specialist has advised you to do so.

Photograph the complete item in indirect daylight against a plain background. If the diamond is mounted, include:

  • A face-up photograph
  • Both side profiles
  • The underside of the setting
  • The inside of the ring
  • Hallmarks and engravings
  • Any visible brand signature
  • Damage, missing stones or previous repairs
  • The complete box and available documents

If the diamond is loose, keep it inside a secure gem container or folded diamond paper. Do not hold it over a hard floor, sink or uncovered surface.

Also upload any receipt, appraisal, insurance schedule, repair record or photograph of the missing report. Even a partial report number may help identify an archived record.

Review My Diamond

A Private and No-Pressure Process

Only information needed to review the item, establish ownership and conduct a secure transaction should be requested.

Uploaded photographs, appraisals and personal documents should be encrypted and limited to authorised reviewers. Personal engravings or identifiable documents should not be used publicly without explicit permission.

Before sending the item, the seller should receive written information about insurance, tracking, inspection, authorised expenses and return arrangements.

Receiving a preliminary indication or final offer does not oblige you to sell.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I legally sell a diamond without a certificate?

A grading report is not generally what establishes your ownership of the diamond. However, you must be legally authorised to sell the item. If ownership is disputed, resolve the matter before transferring it.

Will Sothis Diamonds buy every uncertified diamond?

No. Every item remains subject to physical verification, condition, marketability and Sothis Diamonds’ current buying criteria.

Is the initial review free?

Yes. The initial review and market-based offer should be free and carry no obligation to sell. Any optional laboratory, shipping, removal or third-party expense must be explained separately.

Is an online offer final?

An online figure is normally preliminary. A final offer can be confirmed after the diamond’s identity, origin, quality, condition and documentation have been physically verified.

Does no certificate mean my diamond is worthless?

No. The missing document does not physically change a genuine diamond. However, additional testing, grading uncertainty and associated costs may affect the selling process and offer.

Can I sell a loose diamond without a certificate?

Yes. A loose diamond can be weighed and examined directly, although further testing or grading may still be required.

Can I sell a diamond ring without a certificate?

Yes. Submit the complete ring first. The diamond, setting, smaller stones, precious metal and overall condition can all be considered.

Should I remove the diamond from its ring?

No. Do not remove it yourself. Submit the complete piece so a professional can first decide whether removal is necessary or commercially sensible.

Should I obtain a new GIA report before contacting Sothis?

Not automatically. Begin with a free initial review. The cost and commercial benefit of new grading should be considered before the diamond is submitted.

Can a lost GIA report be replaced?

GIA states that it does not issue duplicate reports. If the report number is known, its information may be available through GIA Report Check, and reports dated after 1 July 2010 may have a downloadable PDF.

Can an HRD Antwerp report be recovered?

Potentially. HRD Antwerp maintains an online report archive and currently offers certain duplicate or update services. Availability should be confirmed using the specific report number.

What if I do not know the report number?

Submit the diamond and any remaining documents. A girdle inscription may help identify an old report, but the stone may need to be assessed as undocumented if no reliable record can be found.

Is a receipt the same as a diamond certificate?

No. A receipt records a transaction. It does not independently verify the diamond’s current quality characteristics.

Is an insurance valuation enough?

It may provide background, but it does not establish the resale offer. Insurance values commonly relate to retail replacement rather than current secondary-market demand.

Can I sell an inherited diamond without paperwork?

Yes. Preserve any old box, photograph, receipt, valuation or repair record and confirm that you have authority to sell the inherited property.

Can I sell a laboratory-grown diamond without its report?

You can submit it for review, but laboratory-grown diamonds are considered within their own resale market and current buying criteria.

Can Sothis tell whether my diamond is natural?

Specialist screening and, when necessary, laboratory testing can help establish whether a diamond is natural or laboratory-grown. Visual appearance alone should not be treated as conclusive.

Can I sell a chipped uncertified diamond?

Potentially. Its condition, possible recutting risk and remaining marketability must be examined.

How quickly will I receive an offer?

The timeframe depends on the available information and whether physical inspection, professional removal or laboratory testing is required. The expected process should be explained after the initial review.

Can I visit Sothis Diamonds in Antwerp?

Yes. Arrange a private appointment in advance so the appropriate specialist is available.

Receive a Free Offer Without a Diamond Certificate

Your diamond may have no paperwork, an old appraisal or only a partially remembered report number. You can still begin with the information available today.

Submit clear photographs of the diamond or complete jewellery item. Include any receipt, valuation, box or document you still possess.

If the item meets the current buying criteria, Sothis Diamonds can advise whether a private Antwerp appointment or an agreed insured shipping process is the appropriate next step.

After physical verification, you can receive a market-based offer that you remain free to accept or decline.
